browser.value: Cloud browser gives ChatGPT Work its own browser on a separate computer in the cloud. It can read pages, click buttons, enter information into forms, and carry out steps on supported public and signed-in websites. ChatGPT may use a connected app or plugin, the cloud browser, or both. It does not use the user's local browser tabs, history, saved passwords, cookies, extensions, or existing sign-ins. Dots also have their own cloud computer and cloud browser; introducing dots says you can open your dot's computer to inspect its work. Local computer access is optional and starts turned off; with it enabled, a dot can use your local browser when its cloud browser is blocked.

schedule_or_away.value: Work / cloud browser: cloud-browser tasks can start on web or mobile and keep working after the user leaves the conversation or closes the computer; they pause when input, sign-in, or confirmation is needed. ChatGPT can run one-time or recurring scheduled tasks, monitor for changes, and respond to supported app events. Event-triggered webhook-based tasks run in Work for supported Gmail, Slack, or GitHub activity on eligible paid plans. Tasks are managed at chatgpt.com/schedules. Dots: official pages describe dots as always-on agents that keep making progress between conversations, 24/7, on their own cloud computer, including after you close your laptop. You can ask a dot to set a reminder or run a recurring check; scheduled runs and proactive updates appear in the conversation and can be managed in Recent activity or the Scheduled section in ChatGPT. When you are not actively working with it, a dot can do 'proactive research' using already-connected apps with tools restricted to be read-only (they cannot send messages, change app content, or control a browser or computer). Authorized background tasks still follow ordinary action rules and safety checks.

memory.value: The pricing page lists Memory, including Memory with past chats (Limited on Free) and Memory sources. Dots share memory with ChatGPT: a dot can receive memories and recent conversation context from ChatGPT, and conversations with a dot can contribute to ChatGPT Memory. Turning off Memory in ChatGPT stops that sharing but does not delete information the dot already received. A dot can retain context from conversations and plugins for as long as the dot is kept; deleting the dot starts deletion of its own context. The dot's context does not retain credentials, images, or screenshots. A dot receives memories from ChatGPT and can create its own memories, including from connected apps. Official help says you currently cannot view, delete, or directly modify individual dot memories; deleting the dot starts deletion of its own context. Disconnecting a plugin stops new access but does not delete information the dot has already built into its context. Files, Codex threads, and ChatGPT conversations a dot created are stored separately and are not deleted when the dot is deleted. ChatGPT memories remain and are managed in ChatGPT Memory settings.
memory.note: Shared-memory behavior was already sourced to this dots privacy FAQ. Additional deletion and plugin-disconnect rules are from the same article and https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001530-getting-started-with-your-dot.

approvals.value: Work / cloud browser: by default ChatGPT asks permission before accessing a new website, with Always ask, Auto approve, or Always allow site-access settings. Website access permission is separate from approval for consequential actions. ChatGPT is designed to request confirmation before hard-to-reverse financial, legal, account, or other real-world commitments, such as confirming a booking or making a payment. Sign-in uses a secure form; credentials are not visible to the model and are not stored. Users can take over the cloud browser. Scheduled tasks that send a message or change external data may require approval, and the task pauses until reviewed. Dots: official help says a dot comes with strong defaults for which actions need approval each time, which can be approved in advance, and which can run without asking. Custom Rules can set 'Take action without asking', 'Take action if pre-approved', 'Ask before taking action', or 'Hand off to you'. Custom Rules cannot turn off core safety requirements (such as taking over to change a password), Auto-review, or restrictions on proactive research. The most sensitive actions, such as changing a password or transferring money, require the user to take over. Other actions such as permanently deleting data or installing software may require approval each time. Approving one message does not give a dot ongoing permission to contact people. Auto-review checks certain planned actions against instructions, Custom Rules, and safety requirements.
approvals.note: Cloud-browser approval settings are from https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001280-using-cloud-browser-in-chatgpt. Custom Rules option labels are from https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001530-getting-started-with-your-dot. Language previously taken only from the retired ChatGPT agent help article (watch mode, screenshot pause during takeover) was removed.

training_on_your_data.value: Dots, official privacy FAQ: for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces, OpenAI does not use your data to train models by default. For personal ChatGPT plans, the 'Improve the model for everyone' setting controls whether a dot's conversations and work may be used to improve models, which may include actions dots take, work they delegate to other agents, automations you set up, and data from connected apps used to inform conversations. OpenAI says it takes steps to remove personal identifiers where possible before using eligible data. It does not train directly on proactive background research or its notes; if a dot brings information from that research into an eligible conversation or task, that information may be used for training depending on settings. Human review may still occur in limited circumstances, including safety-related cases, even when model improvement is turned off. This field no longer uses screenshot or 'agent-mode session' training language from the retired ChatGPT agent help article.
training_on_your_data.note: The same default for Business, Enterprise, and Edu, and the personal-plan control for dots, also appear on https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/. retention.value: Dots: a dot can retain context from conversations and plugins for as long as you keep the dot. Deleting the dot starts deletion of its own context. Information the dot has shared with ChatGPT Memory is managed separately in ChatGPT Memory settings. Official help says a dot's context does not retain credentials, images, or screenshots. Files a dot creates or uses in ChatGPT Library, on your computer, or in a connected storage service follow that location's retention policies; deleting a Library file does not by itself delete a copy already attached to the dot's conversation. Content is encrypted in storage and in transit. In an eligible Enterprise workspace with Enterprise Key Management, long-term data in new dots supports customer-managed encryption keys. Pausing a dot or removing workspace access does not delete the dot's stored information. Work / cloud browser: website information follows ChatGPT data-control settings; cookies and sessions can be cleared in Settings > Cloud browser. A numeric 90-day deletion window for chats and screenshots appeared only on the retired ChatGPT agent help page and is not recorded here as a confirmed current Work or dots retention period.
retention.note: Cloud-browser cookie and session controls are from https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001280-using-cloud-browser-in-chatgpt.

Dots: create and use a dot in the ChatGPT mobile app on iOS or Android, the desktop app (including Windows), or desktop web; dots are not supported on mobile web. In the section on deleting remote data or turning off task mode, help text says schedules will not run if task mode is off or the device is off. Official examples include a daily morning briefing across email and calendar. The Gemini app on Mac can be asked to take action on the Mac from another device if tasks are set up.

memory.value: Tasks can use Personal Intelligence, chats, Connected Apps, skills, location, and websites the user is signed into. The Gemini Apps Privacy Hub describes Memory and Personal Intelligence personalization settings, a Memory summary setting, and the ability to manage info the user asked Gemini to save. History (Keep Activity / History on) is required to assign tasks.

approvals.value: Gemini is designed to pause and check before critical steps, including confirmation or pre-approval before clicking Buy; routine trusted actions can be set to Always allow. After an initial web-browsing permission, for every task that involves web browsing, Gemini will ask for confirmation first, per help. Very sensitive actions require permission each time even if preferences are updated. Built-in safety checks can still pause and ask even when an action or browser permission is set to Always allow. Gemini may ask the user to take control to enter passwords or payment details. Sign-in uses confirmation for Sign in with Google or Password Manager credentials. Shared Doc, Sheet, or Slide edits require review and confirmation. An exception is stated: Gemini can perform bulk actions on private tasks in Google Tasks without confirmation. The blog says businesses are told Gemini is AI when it places calls, and that Gemini will not give out payment or private account info unless the user says so. Calling through Gemini is not currently available in Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska.

where_it_runs.value: The official blog says that when a task is assigned, Gemini uses Google Cloud's Agent Compute Engine to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine dedicated to the user's account and never shared with other users; each VM is sandboxed. Help says tasks can also use local Chrome on desktop or a remote browser on a remote computer. Remote browser and computer data, including auth cookies, is saved for convenience until inactivity or manual delete. Platforms for assigning tasks are the Gemini mobile app, the Gemini app on Mac, and gemini.google.com.

The hub states Google uses the content of future chats to train generative AI models unless the user changes that setting. If the setting is off, future chats will not be used to train generative AI models unless the user provides feedback, but chats may still be reviewed and used to improve Google services in other ways and to protect Google, users, and the public. Temporary chats are not used to train Google's AI models. If History is off and the user does not submit feedback, Google also does not use future chats to train generative AI models. Human reviewers, including service-provider reviewers, review some collected data. Settings do not stop processing chats to create anonymized data to improve Google services. Remote browser and remote computer data is used consistently with the Privacy Notice and is not deleted by deleting Gemini history.

Chats reviewed by service providers are separated from the account and kept for up to 3 years. Remote browser and remote computer data remains until a period of inactivity or until the user manually clears it; deleting Gemini history does not delete that data. Turning off task mode pauses schedules and tasks but does not delete past history, threads, or files Gemini updated.

If Gmail or Outlook is also connected, the Bot asks which account to send from. The starter Bot Tradbot watches personal email and calendar, drafts replies, and never sends without the user. Browser cookies and signed-in sessions persist and are shared across all Bots on the account. Users can watch clicks and typing, or take control for SSO, passkeys, CAPTCHAs, and similar steps.

files.value: The cloud computer has a filesystem; files are visible to every Bot on the account. Bots can run commands on the user's local Mac or Windows computer only if that capability is enabled (default: Ask every time). Sensitive project files are described as living under /workspace on the cloud computer.

messaging.value: Bots work in Slack like a teammate: users can ask questions, hand off work, or loop a Bot into a thread. Docs also describe X Chat. Users can connect Slack as an app. A Bot can be invited to Google Meet or Zoom: it listens, jumps into chat when it can help, and follows through after.

payments.value: At checkout, a Bot can use a card saved in Vault, a card entered in a Secure Form, or a connected wallet such as Link, X Money, or Shop Pay (see Pay for things, referenced from the computer-and-apps page). A card saved in Vault fills in at checkout without a separate approval each time; to approve every payment, the docs say not to save the card. Purchases and financial transfers are listed as actions that should have explicit approval boundaries. In Grok Bot app chats, a Bot can see the number and security code of a card saved in Vault so it can type them at checkout.

schedule_or_away.value: Work continues on the cloud computer while the laptop is closed, 24/7, even when the Grok Bot app is closed. Getting-started docs: after a task is right, ask the Bot to do it on a schedule and it becomes a routine. Mobile apps can pause or resume routines. Approval cards raised by a routine or incoming message expire after 30 minutes if unanswered.

memory.value: Marketing and getting-started docs: Bots keep context from conversations, learn how the team works, and can be asked to remember how the work should be done. Saved to memory is shown as a product behavior. A Bot with one job builds more useful context than a catch-all helper.

approvals.value: Auto Review is on by default. It checks actions before a Bot runs a command, uses a connected app, or uses its computer. Most actions run on their own, but when one needs approval the Bot shows an approval card (Allow once, Always allow, Deny). Custom Rules: up to 20 Allow automatically and 20 Ask first rules; Ask first wins if both match. Built-in safety checks always apply. Team admins can require Auto Review and lock rules. Email sending rules are as described under email. Passwords are filled via Vault, a password manager such as 1Password, or a Secure Form without being shown to the model. Official docs say not to put passwords or payment details in ordinary chat. Local-computer execution defaults to Ask every time.

where_it_runs.value: Bots share one persistent cloud computer assigned to the user account, with a browser, command line, and filesystem. Each user's computer is dedicated and hardware-isolated. Each Bot gets its own screen on that shared computer and can work in parallel. Optional execution on the user's local Mac or Windows computer is separate and defaults to Ask every time. Optional use of apps on the user's phone is mentioned, and team caps apply. Grok Bot needs cloud data storage and does not support Legacy Privacy Mode.

training_on_your_data.value: The x.ai/bot FAQ says Grok Bot uses the same Cursor SSO, auth, and privacy mode; the cloud computer is encrypted in transit and at rest, with training opt-out. Privacy and data-sharing choices are managed through Cursor account settings and, when required, the Grok Bot access flow.

retention.value: Deleting a Bot does not remove shared-computer files or browser sessions. Backend retention and account deletion follow the applicable Cursor terms. Users are instructed to sign out of websites, uninstall connectors, and remove sensitive files when access should end. A more specific retention period in days was not stated on the pages fetched today.

email.value: Connectors can include email (example: Connect my Gmail). Connecting email may allow Muse to read new emails to help keep up with what is important; Muse will not download the whole inbox unless asked; users can manage whether Muse can read new emails in Settings. By default Muse will not take many important actions, like sending an email, without approval. Muse can also have its own @muse.ai email address, separate from the personal inbox; sending from that address requires approval. Users can verify an email address they own so instructions forwarded to Muse are recognized, which does not by itself grant inbox access. Muse may refuse sensitive email requests about financial information, health information, and credentials.

browser.value: A web browser inside the Muse chat can be controlled by the user or Muse, similarly to Chrome or Safari. Documented tasks include booking appointments, making purchases, filling out online forms, and watching for things like price drops. An optional Muse Chrome Extension puts Muse in Chrome's side panel and browses using the user's personal Chrome, only in Muse's tab group. When using the user's Chrome, Muse cannot see saved passwords, browsing history, or Chrome settings; it can use sites the user is already logged into.

The privacy policy allows adding Muse to the same account as Facebook, Instagram, Threads, or WhatsApp; if Muse is added to a different account, Muse will not share Muse interactions or VM data with those Products. Custom connectors can be created for services not in the list.

payments.value: The in-chat browser can make purchases on the user's behalf. Muse is designed to ask for confirmation before important browser actions like making a purchase. Credentials are stored in a Secure Credentials Store so the model does not see passwords.

schedule_or_away.value: The Muse Privacy Policy lists scheduled tasks among stored information, along with saved preferences, goals, and memories, which confirms that scheduled tasks exist. Calendar connectors can update Muse automatically when the schedule changes, and email connectors may share new mail proactively. Detailed official documentation of unattended execution, for example whether work continues if the app is closed, was not fetched as a dedicated help article today.

memory.value: Muse keeps information on the user's isolated virtual machine. Users can ask Muse to forget interactions or use a Forget skill for topics or people; Muse forgets to the best of its ability. Users can ask what Muse remembers or view files like MEMORY.md. After deleting a message or file, Muse may still remember information it learned unless the user uses Forget. Resetting Muse deletes all Muse data. Information previously used with a disconnected connector may remain in memories and conversation history.

approvals.value: By default, Muse will not take many important actions, like sending an email, without approval. Many connectors can be set to retrieve-only, for example with no sending of a calendar invite. Users can change when Muse asks for approval in Settings. Muse is designed to ask before important browser actions such as making a purchase; users can review, allow, or deny, take control of the browser, or stop the task. Web access default settings live under Permissions in Settings. Approval checks for important actions are described as enforced outside the AI model. Muse may ask for extra confirmation on sensitive topics over email.

where_it_runs.value: Muse runs on a cloud virtual machine isolated so no one else's agent can access it; Muse also maintains backups. A built-in web browser runs in that environment. The Chrome extension runs in the user's Chrome, in the Muse tab group only. Devices can include a laptop with Muse for Mac, AI Glasses, and Muse Charm where available. A future Muse Confidential virtual machine is described as in design to keep information private even from Meta. It is not described as self-hosted.

training_on_your_data.value: The Muse Privacy Policy, effective November 16, 2026, supplements the Meta Privacy Policy and takes precedence if they conflict. Users decide whether interactions with Muse can be used to train and improve Meta AI models. This setting is on when the user first uses Muse and can be changed anytime under Settings > Data controls. When off, interactions are not used for future development and improvement, and the change also applies to previous interactions. If training is allowed, Meta says it still removes certain categories of personally identifiable information, such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, and Social Security Numbers, and disassociates interactions from the account. The same toggle covers information from Connectors and Devices and communications Muse has with other people on the user's behalf. Muse does not share conversations or VM data with Meta ad systems, even if Accounts Center includes other Meta Products. If Muse is in the same Accounts Center as other Products, Meta may otherwise combine and use information across profiles and devices except where this policy says data will not be used.

retention.value: Users can delete messages, Side Chats, and VM files, or reset Muse to delete all Muse data. After deletion, memories may remain until the Forget skill is used. Disconnecting a connector stops future data exchange, but previously used information may remain in memories and history. A numeric server-side retention period after account deletion was not stated on the pages fetched today.
